did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm begins with the heading, “For the director of music, according to ‘The Doe of the Dawn’; a psalm of David.” From the text itself, it is clear that this is a musical or traditional heading for the psalm, and it also indicates its connection to David.

Did you know? The psalm opens with a direct cry to the LORD: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” It goes on to describe the worshiper calling out to him both day and night, yet feeling no answer or relief.

Did you know? Alongside the feeling of silence, the worshiper emphasizes that the LORD is “holy” and “enthroned on the praises of Israel”—meaning that his holiness is also connected with the prayers and praise of the people of Israel.

Did you know? The worshiper strengthens his faith by remembering the ancestors: they trusted in the LORD, cried out to him, and were delivered. In this way, the nation’s memory becomes a source of hope in a time of personal distress.

Did you know? The speaker describes himself in stark terms as “a worm and not a man,” and says that everyone who sees him mocks him. This description emphasizes the depth of the humiliation and loneliness he is experiencing.

Did you know? In the midst of his suffering, the worshiper remembers his relationship with the LORD from birth: the LORD brought him out of his mother’s womb and has been his trust. This memory stands alongside his plea not to be far from him in his time of trouble.
Did you know? The enemies are portrayed through a series of animal images: bulls, a lion, and dogs. These images present them as a threatening force surrounding the worshiper on every side.

Did you know? The psalm also describes the distress through physical sensations: the body is falling apart, the heart melts, and strength dries up. In this way, emotional suffering and external danger are presented as a tangible physical experience.

Did you know? Among the descriptions of danger, the psalm also mentions the dividing of the garments and casting lots for the clothing. This detail deepens the sense of helplessness, as though the worshiper is already regarded by his enemies as their spoil.

Did you know? In its final section, the psalm expands from personal distress to a universal vision: the ends of the earth and the families of the nations will remember the LORD, turn back to him, and bow before him. The ending emphasizes the LORD’s kingship and the passing on of the story of his righteousness to future generations.
